issues.title: Popular proxy software Xray-core covered up a certification verification bypass vulnerability for half a year
issues.body:
Disclaimer: I am the reporter of the vulnerability.

Xray-core maintainers look down on "skip certificate verification" feature (i.e. the `allowInsecure` option in Xray-core) or similar options in proxy software, arguing that this is equivalent to having no security measures at all and leaves users "streaking", exposing them to the risk of man-in-the-middle attacks. However, if a vulnerability in Xray-core itself causes users to be "streaking" and fall victim to man-in-the-middle attacks, Xray-core will cover it up and act as if nothing has happened.

On [October 21, 2021](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/commit/acb81ebe3de44e7ca197bf079f1d1122ff49b490), the `pinnedPeerCertificateChainSha256` option, with no known issues, was added to Xray-core. This provides a double layer of security: if this option is enabled, custom certificate chain pinning logic will be performed in addition to the regular certificate verification. This also facilitates the use of self-signed certificates: to use a self-signed certificate securely, a user can enable both `allowInsecure` and `pinnedPeerCertificateChainSha256` to skip the regular certificate verification and perform only the custom certificate chain pinning logic.

However, Xray-core later claimed that `allowInsecure` is insecure and enabling `allowInsecure` is like "streaking" and would leave users vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.

On [January 9, 2026](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/commit/0ca13452b8e99824e08c2c860dd0f84a4ae2859d), Xray-core removed `pinnedPeerCertificateChainSha256` and replaced it with a new option, `pinnedPeerCertSha256`, to stop users from skipping certificate verification (or so-called "streaking"). For self-signed certificates, both `allowInsecure` and `pinnedPeerCertSha256` must be enabled, which skips the regular certificate verification and only performs the custom certificate pinning logic. This should have helped the users to use self-signed certificates securely. However, `pinnedPeerCertSha256` contains a certificate verification bypass vulnerability.

On [January 13, 2026](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/releases/tag/v26.1.13), Xray-core released the first version containing this certificate verification bypass vulnerability. Since the old option had been removed, users had no choice but to migrate to the new vulnerable option. At this point, the certificate verification defense was already teetering on the brink of collapse. Fortunately, as long as users neither use a self-signed certificate nor enable `allowInsecure`, the regular certificate verification could still provide some protection.

On [January 16, 2026](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/commit/760223ad70f822fcb859a217e60e038a970610f9), Xray-core modified the logic of `pinnedPeerCertSha256`, making it always skip the regular certificate verification and only performs the custom certificate pinning logic. This means a protection layer has been missing: the regular certificate verification is always skipped. If a verification bypass vulnerability exists in `pinnedPeerCertSha256` (and unfortunately, it does), the custom certificate pinning logic will fail to function, effectively leaving no certificate verification in place, which allows a man-in-the-middle attack to be successfully performed. At this point, the certificate verification defense has completely collapsed.

On February 6, 2026, I found the above certificate verification bypass vulnerability in Xray-core’s `pinnedPeerCertSha256` and privately reported to Xray-core maintainers. A man-in-the-middle attacker could insert a leaf certificate at any place in the certificate chain, and the custom certificate pinning logic would verify the leaf certificate successfully, thereby leading to the success of man-in-the-middle attacks. This is an overly simple vulnerability; even without advanced security knowledge, I was able to discover it at a glance.

issues.title: Analysis of an entropy-related function in QDPI (Qosmos ixEngine)
issues.body:
This is analysis, based on reverse engineering, of an entropy-related subroutine in qdpi_detector, part of Qosmos ixEngine and one of the software libraries found in the [2025 Geedge Networks leak](https://github.com/net4people/bbs/issues/519). I call the function `entropy_score`, because it accepts a byte buffer and returns a score between 0 and 10000 that depends on factors such as the proportion of 0 bits to 1 bits and the number of contiguous runs of bits. The function is called from many places in qdpi_detector, including in contexts that use configuration parameters with names like `"entropy_threshold"`, `"printable_char_seq_threshold"`, and `"char_occur_threshold"`. I was initially attracted to this function because the configuration parameter names [are reminscent](https://github.com/net4people/bbs/issues/519#issuecomment-3439657972) of the documented ["exemptions" to the blocking of fully encrypted traffic in China](https://gfw.report/publications/usenixsecurity23/en/#4), which include "Entropy exemption", "More than 20 contiguous bytes are printable", and "Half of the first packet are printable". After analysis, the precise details of classification do not exactly match up, so I do not think the previously discussed classifier of fully encrypted protocols in China is based on qdpi_detector or the `entropy_score` function. But it is similar in spirit. I've made a commented disassembly of the `entropy_score` function, as well as a translation into C. - [impl.s](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33787102/impl.s.txt) - [entropy.c](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33786954/entropy.c) To compile the code test harness, do this: 
cc -Wall -O2 -g -masm=intel -c -o entropy.o entropy.c
as -g -o impl.o impl.s
cc -Wall -O2 -g -no-pie entropy.o impl.o -o entropy
## Background Among the files of [the Geedge Networks leak of September 2025](https://github.com/net4people/bbs/issues/519), under an "AppSketch" subdirectory, are RPM files of many different versions of a package called "qdpi_detector". The version numbers range from 3.0.2 to 5.0.6. One such RPM file is repo/repo.geedge.net/pulp/content/8/x86_64/stable/AppSketch/Packages/q/qdpi_detector-5.0.6.64c1824-1.el8.x86_64.rpm. The RPMs are binary only, with no source code other than some header files. Even Geedge did not have the source code of QDPI; the InterSecLab report on the Geedge leak [notes](https://interseclab.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/The-Internet-Coup_September2025.pdf#page=23): > Another system for performing deep packet inspection consists of two binary files, named "libqmengine.so" and "libqmbundle.so." While the leaked information does not include the associated source code, it includes Jira tickets that refer to the system as QDPI or "third-party recognition engine library" (第三方识别引擎库), implying that it may not have been developed by Geedge Networks. The Jira tickets analyzed in the data express concerns regarding the inability to modify the behavior of the third-party engine and highlight challenges in obtaining a technical support contact for this system. Such concerns lend further support to the notion that these binaries were not developed by Geedge Networks. You can extract files from the RPMs with the [rpm2cpio](https://man.archlinux.org/man/rpm2cpio.8.en) command. To list the files, use `cpio -t`: 
$ rpm2cpio qdpi_detector-5.0.6.64c1824-1.el8.x86_64.rpm | cpio -t -v

comments.issue_title: Analysis of an entropy-related function in QDPI (Qosmos ixEngine)
comments.body:
> huh, so this is how the GFW is blocking fully encrypted protocols?

On the contrary, the ixEngine function has significant differences from what was documented in ["How the Great Firewall of China Detects and Blocks Fully Encrypted Traffic"](https://gfw.report/publications/usenixsecurity23/en/#4) (2023), which makes me believe that the ixEngine function is *not* what was responsible for that blocking.

Most notably, the Ex1 exemption from 2023 was based in simple population count thresholds: a byte string where between 42.5% and 57.5% of the bits are 1 bits was considered to be high-entropy. The ixEngine function *does* incorporate a population count; but in addition to the raw population count there is a population count of just the most significant bits of each byte; as well there is the computation of the number of bit "runs" in the input, which is a different thing. Then, there is the fact that the population counts and run counts are not used directly, but undergo transformation by the formulas I cited and are then used to look up an opaque "score".

The `entropy_score` function is called from many places in libqmbundle.so (see all the `XREFS: CALL` addresses in the disassembly above). I have not checked those call sites, but my guess is that the function is used as a common subroutine by several different classifiers that rely on some kind of randomness detection. It's not only used for the overall "high_entropy" protocol classification result.

> should probably test this on packets from protocols like Shadowsocks to see how they blocked it

That's a good idea, testing some real protocol payloads and seeing what score `entropy_score` assigns them. It's just a guess, but `processed_bytes_limit` = 256 may mean that only the first 256 payload bytes are processed, by default. (Which may mitigate the integer overflow issues the function has.)

# admin: `addPeer` can dial any unix socket and report the result in `last_error`

**Version:** yggdrasil-go `v0.5.14` (`422836ee`), also present in `develop` at the time of writing
**Surface:** admin API (`addPeer`, `getPeers`) — reachable by anyone who can open the admin socket
(unix, group-writable `0660`) or the admin TCP listener when configured
**Not a wire-protocol issue:** no remote peer is involved; this is a local admin capability

## Summary

`addPeer` accepts any URI, and the `unix` scheme is a legitimate link type
(`src/core/link.go:613`). The dialer takes the path straight from the URL
(`src/core/link_unix.go:34-38`):

```go
addr, err := net.ResolveUnixAddr("unix", url.Path)
...
return l.dialer.DialContext(ctx, "unix", addr.String())
```

The result of that dial is surfaced verbatim by `getPeers`
(`src/admin/getpeers.go:64-67`: `peer.LastError = p.LastError.Error()`).

Combined, these two facts give a caller a filesystem/network oracle:

| URI passed to `addPeer` | `addPeer` | `getPeers` → `last_error` |
|---|---|---|
| `unix:///etc/passwd` | accepted | `dial unix /etc/passwd: connect: permission denied` |
| `unix:///nonexistent` | accepted | `connect: no such file or directory` |
| `unix:///run/other.sock` | accepted | `invalid handshake, remote side is not Yggdrasil` |
| `tcp://127.0.0.1:18081` (closed) | accepted | `connect: connection refused` |
| `tcp://10.255.255.1:80` | accepted | `dial tcp ...: i/o timeout` |
| `tcp://no-such-host.invalid:443` | accepted | `lookup ... on 10.64.0.1:53: no such host` |

The last row leaks the resolver actually in use (in our run the host's internal DNS address), and
`i/o timeout` vs `connection refused` distinguishes "filtered" from "closed" — the classic
port-scanner primitive, reachable through the admin socket instead of the network.

`file://` and other unsupported schemes are correctly rejected by `dialerFor`
(`src/core/link.go:605-622`, `ErrLinkUnrecognisedSchema`), so the issue is **not** a missing
scheme allowlist — it is the combination of (a) `unix://` with an arbitrary path and (b) raw
error text in the admin response.

## Why this is a defect rather than a design decision

- The admin API is documented as control of the local node, not as a general-purpose dialer:
  `addPeer` exists to add *peers*, and the unix scheme is meant for local overlay endpoints
  (e.g. a local sidecar), not for probing arbitrary paths.
- `last_error` is meant to tell an operator why a configured peer is down. It is not meant to be
  an error-text channel that distinguishes "path exists but not a socket" from "path does not
  exist" for arbitrary paths chosen by the caller.
- Neither behaviour is needed for any legitimate `addPeer` use: a legitimate operator passes a
  path they control and can test it themselves.

## Impact

Local information disclosure and network probing by any principal that can talk to the admin
socket. It does not by itself give code execution or break the overlay, but:

- it turns a read-mostly operator interface into a probe of local services (unix sockets:
  Docker/containerd, ssh-agent, dbus, systemd private sockets, application sockets);
- it discloses whether firewall rules drop or reject, and which resolver the node uses;
- it composes with the missing request limits: a caller can queue many dial attempts.

Severity in our assessment: **low-medium** (requires admin access, which is already powerful),
but the fix is cheap and removes a class of surprising capability.

## Proposed direction (design, not a finished patch)

Two separable changes; the first can ship alone:

1. **Classifier instead of raw text** in `getPeers`: map `LastError` to a small enum
   (`refused | timeout | no_route | dns_failure | not_yggdrasil | path_denied | path_missing`),
   optionally keep the raw text behind a debug flag. This alone removes the DNS-address leak and
   most of the oracle value, and it is a strict improvement for operators (a stable token is

issues.title: Admin API: explicit null arguments can terminate the daemon
issues.body:
An admin request with explicit `"arguments": null` can terminate the daemon with a nil-pointer panic. I reproduced this against `develop` at `6ad41376b69c1fa223dfacf577a6f947ca39de6c` and verified a small local fix.

### Reproduction

Start a disposable daemon built from that revision with `-useconf`, supplying this configuration on stdin:

```json
{
  "AdminListen": "tcp://127.0.0.1:19001",
  "IfName": "none",
  "MulticastInterfaces": [],
  "Peers": [],
  "Listen": []
}
```

Once the admin endpoint is listening, send:

```python
import socket

with socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 19001), timeout=2) as client:
    client.sendall(b'{"request":"getPeers","arguments":null}\n')
    print(client.recv(4096))
```

**Actual:** the connection closes and the daemon terminates with a nil-pointer panic (exit code 2 in my Windows reproduction).

**Expected:** an invalid admin request should receive a JSON error response without terminating the daemon. A connection using `keepalive` should remain usable for a subsequent valid request.

I also reproduced the same null-pointer failure for `addPeer` and `removePeer` in local handler tests. This requires access to the admin endpoint; I have not established reachability through ordinary overlay peer traffic.

### Cause and proposed fix

The handlers allocate a request pointer and then call `json.Unmarshal(in, &req)`. JSON `null` sets that pointer to nil, after which handlers such as `getPeersHandler` dereference it. The default `{}` assigned in `handleRequest` only covers omitted arguments, not an explicit null value.

Relevant source: [admin request decoding and dispatch](https://github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/blob/6ad41376b69c1fa223dfacf577a6f947ca39de6c/src/admin/admin.go), [getPeers handler](https://github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/blob/6ad41376b69c1fa223dfacf577a6f947ca39de6c/src/admin/getpeers.go).

My local fix adds the `bytes` import and rejects explicit null immediately before calling `handler.handler(req.Arguments)` in `handleRequest`:

```go
// Null would clear the request pointers allocated by handlers.
if bytes.Equal(bytes.TrimSpace(req.Arguments), []byte("null")) {
    return errors.New("arguments must not be null")
}
```

Omitted arguments retain the existing `{}` default. Ordinary object arguments remain unchanged.

### Local verification

- Regression tests fail for null arguments on the original code and pass with the guard. They cover omitted arguments, empty/nonempty objects, null with whitespace, rejection before dispatch, and `getPeers`/`addPeer`/`removePeer` followed by a valid request on the same keepalive connection.
- With the fix, a real Windows daemon returned errors for all three null commands, stayed alive, and accepted subsequent valid commands on the same connection. TUN, discovery and peers were disabled for this reproduction.
- Go 1.26.9, Windows amd64: build, `go vet ./...`, and the selected test suite passed.
- Go 1.26.9, Linux amd64 (Alpine 3.24.2 under WSL2, GCC 15.2.0, CGO enabled): the full suite and full race suite passed, each with 67 tests/subtests and no test skips or race reports. Commands were `go test -count=1 -timeout=180s -parallel=2 ./...` and `go test -race -count=1 -timeout=300s -parallel=2 ./...`, with `GOFLAGS=-p=1`. These ran in a network namespace with loopback only and no external route.

These are local results, not GitHub CI results or a claim of validation on every supported platform. I searched existing issues/PRs and checked the relevant changes in #1364 and #1365; I did not find a matching null-argument fix.

issues.title: yggdrasilctl exits successfully after a recovered fatal error
issues.body:
`yggdrasilctl` exits with status **0** after recovering a panic and printing `Fatal error`. This makes shell scripts and monitoring treat a failed admin command as successful.

I reproduced this on `develop` at `6ad41376b69c1fa223dfacf577a6f947ca39de6c` with Go 1.26.9 on Windows/amd64. The same recovery path handles connection failures, invalid JSON and errors decoding typed responses.

### Minimal reproduction

Build the unmodified console:

```sh
go build -o yggdrasilctl ./cmd/yggdrasilctl
```

Run it against an invalid local TCP destination; no daemon is needed:

```sh
./yggdrasilctl -endpoint=tcp://127.0.0.1:0 getSelf
echo $?
```

PowerShell equivalent:

```powershell
.\yggdrasilctl.exe -endpoint=tcp://127.0.0.1:0 getSelf
$LASTEXITCODE
```

**Actual:** a `Fatal error: dial tcp ...` message, followed by exit status `0`.
**Expected:** a nonzero exit status, consistent with other admin command errors.
The exact dial error wording is platform-dependent.

### Cause and minimal proposed change

In [cmd/yggdrasilctl/main.go](https://github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/blob/6ad41376b69c1fa223dfacf577a6f947ca39de6c/cmd/yggdrasilctl/main.go#L33-L50), the deferred recovery function returns `1`, but that return value is discarded. After recovery, `run()` returns its zero result and `main()` passes it to `os.Exit`.

A named result lets the deferred function set the actual exit status while retaining deferred cleanup:

```diff
-func run() int {
+func run() (exitCode int) {
 	logbuffer := &bytes.Buffer{}
 	logger := log.New(logbuffer, "", log.Flags())
 
-	defer func() int {
+	defer func() {
 		if r := recover(); r != nil {
 			logger.Println("Fatal error:", r)
 			fmt.Print(logbuffer)
-			return 1
+			exitCode = 1
 		}
-		return 0
 	}()
```

### Local validation of the proposed change

I added subprocess regression tests that invoke the real `main()` and inspect the OS exit status. Before the change, connection failure, invalid JSON, and a malformed typed response all incorrectly returned `0`. After the change, all three return `1`.

Five additional cases verify unchanged behavior: API errors with and without an error message return `1`; a successful JSON response, version output and usage output return `0`.

- Windows/amd64: all eight cases pass; console build and `go vet ./cmd/yggdrasilctl` pass. A separate run of the built executable confirms failure status `1` and version status `0`.
- Linux/amd64 (Alpine 3.24.2, Go 1.26.9, GCC 15.2.0): `go test -json -count=1 -timeout=180s -parallel=2 ./...` and `go test -race -json -count=1 -timeout=300s -parallel=2 ./...` pass with `GOMAXPROCS=2` and `GOFLAGS=-p=1`. Each run records 67 passing test/subtest events, zero skips/failures and no race reports.
- Linux tests ran in an isolated network namespace with loopback only. This is local validation, not an upstream CI run or a live mesh test; native Windows race and other OS integration checks were not run.

I searched open and closed issues/PRs for `yggdrasilctl`, exit status/code, `Fatal error` and recovery. I did not find a matching report. Historical #641 introduced the `run()`/`os.Exit` structure but does not resolve this recovery result. This is separate from the admin daemon crash reported in #1387.

issues.title: core: close the per-dial transport of ws/wss dials
issues.body:
## Summary

When a ws/wss dial is cancelled or times out, `net/http` may keep finishing the dial in the background and park the connection in the transport's idle pool. Each dial creates its own `http.Transport` and drops it afterwards, so these sockets stay open after the dial has returned: a cancelled WS dial left its socket open for more than 10 s in testing, and a WSS dial keeps it until the TLS handshake timeout.

## Fix

Defer `CloseIdleConnections()` on the per-dial transport in `src/core/link_ws.go` and `src/core/link_wss.go`. It closes idle connections and cancels dials still in progress. The upgraded connection is not in the pool and is not affected (`TestWSDialTimeoutSparesUpgradedConn` from #1381 keeps passing).

## Test

`TestDialCancelClosesSocket` cancels ws, wss and socks dials stuck in the handshake and requires each to return and close its socket within a second:

- without the change: ws and wss fail (socket left open), socks passes;
- with the change: all pass.

`go test ./...` passes; the dial tests also pass under `-race`.

This builds on #1381 and includes its commit until that is merged; only the last commit is new.

issues.title: Mobile nodes ignore `GroupPassword`, `NodeInfo` and `NodeInfoPrivacy`
issues.body:
# Mobile nodes ignore `GroupPassword`, `NodeInfo` and `NodeInfoPrivacy`

## Version / commit

- `yggdrasil-go` tag `v0.5.14` (`b99b1804`), file `contrib/mobile/mobile.go`.
- Line numbers below are from that commit; `develop` was not checked (no network access
  from the machine the patch was prepared on).
- Desktop reference: `cmd/yggdrasil/main.go` at the same commit.

## Summary

The mobile entry point (`contrib/mobile`, used by the Android and iOS apps through
`gomobile bind`) builds the list of `core.SetupOption` values by hand. Three options that
the desktop daemon passes are missing:

| Option | Desktop (`cmd/yggdrasil/main.go`) | Mobile (`contrib/mobile/mobile.go`) |
|---|---|---|
| `core.GroupPassword` | `:214-215` | never passed |
| `core.NodeInfo` | `:202` | never passed |
| `core.NodeInfoPrivacy` | `:203` | never passed |

The same JSON configuration therefore behaves differently on a phone and on a desktop
node, with no error, no log line and no API surface where the application could notice.

## Steps to reproduce (static, no device needed)

```sh
$ cd yggdrasil-go-0.5.14
$ grep -n 'core\.\(NodeInfo\|NodeInfoPrivacy\|GroupPassword\)' cmd/yggdrasil/main.go
202:			core.NodeInfo(cfg.NodeInfo),
203:			core.NodeInfoPrivacy(cfg.NodeInfoPrivacy),
215:			options = append(options, core.GroupPassword(cfg.GroupPassword))

$ grep -n 'core\.\(NodeInfo\|NodeInfoPrivacy\|GroupPassword\)' contrib/mobile/mobile.go
# no output
```

The option block that mobile does build is `contrib/mobile/mobile.go:61-83`:
`PeerFilter`, `Peer`, `Peer`, `AllowedPublicKey`, `ListenAddress` — and then
`core.New(m.config.Certificate, logger, options...)` at `:85`.

That the configuration surface is meant to carry these fields on mobile as well is visible
from the package's own config generator: `GenerateConfigJSON()` (`mobile.go:196`) marshals
the whole `config.NodeConfig`, so a mobile app is offered `GroupPassword`, `NodeInfo` and
`NodeInfoPrivacy` in the config it hands back to `StartJSON`:

```sh
$ go run ./tmp_showjson   # prints mobile.GenerateConfigJSON()
{"...","GroupPassword":"","NodeInfo":null,"NodeInfoPrivacy":false,...}
```

## Steps to reproduce (on a device / emulator)

1. Build the mobile package with `gomobile bind` and start a node with
   `{"GroupPassword":"secret","NodeInfo":{"name":"phone"},"NodeInfoPrivacy":true}`.
2. From a **public** node (no group password), send traffic to the phone's address, or ask
   the phone for its nodeinfo (admin `getNodeInfo`, or `yggdrasilctl getNodeInfo` from a
   peer in the same overlay).
3. Observed on desktop with the same JSON: traffic is dropped and nodeinfo contains
   `{"name":"phone"}`. Observed on mobile: traffic from the public node is accepted and
   nodeinfo contains the defaults (`buildname`, `buildversion`, `buildplatform`,
   `buildarch`) instead of `{"name":"phone"}`.

Step 3 was not executed on a real device in this report (no emulator available), see
"Boundaries". The two prior steps are proven by code and by the unit test added in the PR.

## Impact

- **`GroupPassword` silently does nothing.** `GroupPassword` is the only mechanism that

The QUIC dial builds a per-host TLS config clone and sets `ServerName` on it — but then passes the **base** config (`l.tlsconfig`, without `ServerName`) to `quic.DialAddr`, so:

# Admin socket: requests are read without a size limit or a deadline

## Summary

`src/admin/admin.go` (v0.5.14) accepts a connection and hands it to
`handleRequest`, which creates `json.NewDecoder(conn)` directly on the socket:

* no `io.LimitReader` — the decoder will consume an arbitrarily large amount of
  data (and, for a JSON string/number token, buffer it) before it gives up;
* no `SetReadDeadline` — a connection that sends nothing after connecting is
  serviced by a goroutine that blocks forever;
* `listen()` (`admin.go:288`) starts one goroutine per accepted connection and
  has no cap on concurrent connections;
* there is no authentication (`admin.go:18` is still `// TODO: Add
  authentication`); the unix socket is only protected by its file mode (0660),
  and a `tcp://` admin listener is reachable by anyone who can route to it.

Each of these on its own is enough for a client with access to the admin socket
to make the daemon spend resources it never gets back.

## Measured impact

Both columns are the same binary build from this snapshot, on Linux
(`7.2.11+deb14-amd64`, x86-64, Go 1.27.2), with `IfName: none`, no peers and no
multicast interfaces, so the numbers are only about the admin socket. RSS is
`VmRSS` from `/proc/<pid>/status`, fds are `/proc/<pid>/fd` entries.

| phase | unpatched | patched |
| --- | --- | --- |
| baseline (idle daemon) | 15 872 kB RSS, 6 fds | 18 172 kB RSS, 6 fds |
| one connection sends 64 MiB of `{"request":"AAAA…` | 191 784 kB RSS (+175 MB), no response | 22 964 kB RSS (+4.8 MB), error response, connection closed |
| bytes the client could write before the socket was closed | 64 MiB (all of it) | 1 MiB |
| 100 connections that send nothing, after 2 s | 106 fds | 106 fds |
| the same 100 connections, after 35 s | 106 fds (still open) | 6 fds (all closed) |

Notes:

* The unpatched daemon never answered the flood: the decoder was still waiting
  for the closing quote of the unterminated string after 64 MiB, i.e. the
  payload was held for as long as the client kept the connection open. The
  patched build answered
  `{"status":"error","error":"request too large, limit is 1048576 bytes"}`
  and closed the socket.
* RSS did not come back down after the flooding connection was closed: the
  ~175 MB stayed resident in the unpatched process (Go returns large spans to
  the OS lazily; with a steady stream of connections the allocator keeps
  reusing them, so the high-water mark is what matters for OOM).
* With one goroutine and one fd per connection, 100 silent connections are
  exactly 100 goroutines and 100 fds; the number is limited only by the client.
* `listen()` retries `Accept` on error without any backoff, so once the process
  hits `EMFILE` the accept loop turns into a hot loop. [assumed: `EMFILE` is
  what a local client would hit first on a small device; the non-blocking retry
  is visible in code]

```bash
yggdrasil -genconf -json > cfg.json     # then set AdminListen, IfName: none,
                                        # MulticastInterfaces: [], Peers: []
yggdrasil -useconf < cfg.json &
python3 - <<'PY'

s = socket.socket(socket.AF_UNIX); s.connect("/tmp/admin.sock")
s.sendall(b'{"request":"')
for _ in range(64):                      # 64 MiB, never terminated
    s.sendall(b"A" * (1 << 20))
PY
grep VmRSS /proc/<pid>/status; ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l
```

The admin API is a control plane: it is supposed to accept a small JSON
request, run a handler and answer. `json.Decoder` is a streaming decoder
without an inherent bound, so the daemon implicitly trusts the peer to send a
bounded request, but the peer is not trusted — that is the whole point of the
`admin` group / socket mode. The wire format, the request set and the handlers
are fine; the read path is simply unbounded in bytes and in time.

issues.body:
# admin: limit request size and add read deadline for admin connections

## What this changes

`src/admin/admin.go` only (plus a new `src/admin/admin_test.go`).

1. **Request size limit.** `handleRequest` now decodes through a
   `limitedReader` capped at `maxRequestSize = 1 MiB` per request, instead of
   decoding straight from the `net.Conn`. The reader returns a distinct error
   (`errRequestTooLarge`) instead of `io.EOF` when the budget is exhausted, so
   the handler can tell "too large" from "truncated" and answer with
   `{"status":"error","error":"request too large, limit is 1048576 bytes"}`
   before closing the connection. The budget is reset for every request on a
   keepalive connection, so the limit is per request, not per connection.
2. **Read deadline.** Before each request the connection gets
   `SetReadDeadline(now + requestReadTimeout)` with
   `requestReadTimeout = 30 * time.Second`. A connection that sends nothing (or
   sends an incomplete request and stalls) is answered with
   `{"status":"error","error":"timed out waiting for request"}` and closed.
   The deadline is re-armed per request, so a long-running handler does not
   count against the client's next request.
3. **Errors on the read path are terminal.** `handleRequest` previously kept
   looping if `req.KeepAlive` was true, which a failed decode could not set,
   but a failed decode after an earlier keepalive request could re-enter the
   loop on a broken stream. A decode error now always closes the connection.

Nothing else changed: no new options, no new dependencies, no changes to
handlers, to `AdminSocketRequest`/`AdminSocketResponse`, to the request names
or to the response shape. An oversized or timed-out request is answered with
the existing error response fields.

## Why these values

* **1 MiB per request.** Every request the daemon ships is `{"request": "<name>",
  "arguments": {…}}` where the arguments are a handful of strings (`getPeers`
  with `sort`, `addPeer` with a URI and interface name). The largest realistic
  request is well under 1 KiB, so 1 MiB leaves ~1000x headroom while capping
  what one connection can make the decoder hold at ~1 MiB instead of unbounded
  (a 64 MiB stream took the process from 16 MB to 190 MB RSS in testing).
  Anything that legitimately needs more than 1 MiB per request would have to be
  a new bulk API, and could then be exempted explicitly. If reviewers prefer a
  tighter bound, 64 KiB would still be ~60x the largest real request; the
  constant is in one place.
* **30 s to deliver a request.** `yggdrasilctl` and similar clients dial and
  write the request immediately; 30 s is far above any plausible scheduling or
  connection-setup delay, and it only affects connections that are *silent*.
  It is deliberately longer than typical admin polling intervals but honest
  about the tradeoff: a client that holds a `keepalive` connection and sends
  nothing for more than 30 s will now be disconnected and has to reconnect.
  (Today such a connection lives forever, which is the bug.) If a longer idle
  window is wanted for a specific deployment, making it an option is a
  one-line change; it is a package-level `var` today purely so tests can
  shorten it.
* **Responses are not limited.** The limit is on the request read path, and a
  read deadline does not apply to writes, so large responses (`getTree` on a
  large network, `lookups`) are unaffected. Only reading a request is bounded.

# A QUIC peer that completes the handshake but never opens a stream blocks all other QUIC peers

## Version / commit

- `yggdrasil-go` commit `422836ee` (tag `v0.5.14`), file `src/core/link_quic.go`.
- Line numbers below are from that commit. `develop` still has the same file: blob
  `ffe7a2c8b71198acaba831563bfac27010019f06` for `src/core/link_quic.go@develop` equals the
  blob this patch changes, so the issue is not fixed on `develop` either (checked via the
  GitHub API on 2026-10-22).
- `github.com/quic-go/quic-go v0.60.0` (pinned in `go.mod`).

## Steps to reproduce

1. Start a node with a QUIC listener, e.g. `Listen: ["quic://0.0.0.0:9001"]`.
2. From any host that can reach the port, complete the QUIC handshake and then do
   **nothing** — do not open a stream (`quic.DialAddr` and return; no `OpenStream`).
3. From a second host, connect normally (handshake + open the link stream immediately,
   which is what `linkQUIC.dial` does at `src/core/link_quic.go:64`).

Minimal client for step 2 (quic-go v0.60.0):

```go
conn, err := quic.DialAddr(ctx, "node:9001", tlsConf, &quic.Config{})
// handshake done, deliberately no OpenStream
_ = conn
```

## What happens

The second peer's handshake succeeds and its `OpenStreamSync` returns without error, so
from the peer's point of view the connection is up. But the listener never hands that
connection to the links layer: `links.listen` (`src/core/link.go:446`, accept loop at `:503-511`) stays blocked in
`li.listener.Accept()`, because the single accept goroutine is stuck one connection
earlier. Nothing is logged, no error is returned to the peer — a silent blackhole. All
QUIC peers on that listener are affected, including peers that were already configured.

The node also keeps the blocking connection alive indefinitely: the server-side
`KeepAlivePeriod: 20s` (`src/core/link_quic.go:46`) makes the server itself send PINGs,
which resets the idle timers on both ends, so `MaxIdleTimeout: 1m` never fires. With
`KeepAlivePeriod` set to 0 the block would clear after roughly 60s; with the shipped
configuration it does not clear at all.

TCP, TLS and WS/WSS listeners are not affected — only `quic://`.

## What was expected

A connection is a peer only after it opens the link stream. A connection that never opens
one should be closed (or at least not block the listener), and other peers should be
accepted as usual.

## Why this is not by design

`src/core/link_quic.go:85-106` (v0.5.14):

```go
go func() {
	for {
		qc, err := ql.Accept(ctx)      // :87
		switch err {
		...
		case nil:
			qs, err := qc.AcceptStream(ctx)   // :95  <- blocks here
			if err != nil {
				_ = qc.CloseWithError(1, ...)
				continue
			}
			ch <- &linkQUICStream{...}        // :100 <- unbuffered send
		}
	}
}()
```

- The whole listener has exactly one goroutine, and `AcceptStream` is called from inside
  it, so `ql.Accept` is not reached again until the current peer opens a stream.
- There is no deadline on that wait: `ctx` is the listener context created in
  `src/core/link.go:447` (`context.WithCancel(l.core.ctx)`), which is only cancelled when
  the listener itself is closed. The per-link `SetDeadline` at `src/core/link.go:635`
  never applies, because the connection has not been passed to the links layer yet.
- The `ch` send on line 100 is on an unbuffered channel (`link_quic.go:80`), so even a
  successful `AcceptStream` can stall the same loop while nothing is calling `Accept()`.
- Other transports do not have this shape: `link_tcp`/`link_tls`/`link_ws` hand the
  accepted connection to a fresh goroutine per connection (`src/core/link.go:515`), so a
  stuck peer only costs its own goroutine.

A single unauthenticated TCP connection to the QUIC port is enough; no valid certificate,
key or password is needed, because the handshake is completed before the link layer does
any authentication.

- Any node that exposes a QUIC listener: the first peer that connects and does not open a

  immediately.
- That wait is bounded by `context.WithTimeout(ctx, quicStreamAcceptTimeout)`
  (`quicStreamAcceptTimeout = 10 * time.Second`). If the peer does not open the link
  stream in time, the connection is closed with `qc.CloseWithError(1, ...)`, as it
  already was on a stream error.
- The accepted `linkQUICStream` is handed to the listener channel from that goroutine
  with a `select` on `ctx.Done()`, so the unbuffered `ch` (`link_quic.go:80`) cannot
  stall the accept loop either.
- The per-connection goroutines are cancelled when the accept loop exits (the loop
  derives a cancellable child context and defers the cancel), so closing the listener
  does not leave them waiting for the full timeout.

New test: `src/core/link_quic_test.go`.

## Why this way

- The defect is ordering, not a missing check: one connection in the wrong state consumed
  the only goroutine that could accept the next one. Making the wait concurrent is the
  smallest change that removes that coupling; it is also what the other link types already
  do (`src/core/link.go:515` spawns a goroutine per accepted connection).
- A deadline is needed on top of the goroutine, otherwise a silent peer keeps a
  connection (and its goroutine) alive forever — the server's own `KeepAlivePeriod: 20s`
  prevents `MaxIdleTimeout` from firing.
- 10s is deliberately generous: a real peer opens the stream immediately after the
  handshake (`linkQUIC.dial`, `link_quic.go:64`), so only peers that are not speaking the
  link protocol hit the timeout.
- No refactoring beyond that: the error `switch`, the channel type, `linkQUICListener`, the
  dial path and the link framing are untouched.

## Test

`TestQUICListenerPeerWithoutStream` (`src/core/link_quic_test.go`):

1. starts a real `linkQUIC` listener on `127.0.0.1:0` with a self-signed cert and the same
   `quic.Config` as production (1m idle timeout, 20s keepalive);
2. peer 1 completes the QUIC handshake and opens no stream, then the test waits 500ms so
   the listener is parked waiting for that stream (`AcceptStream` does not return until the
   peer sends something on a stream, which is exactly the blocking state);
3. peer 2 completes the handshake, calls `OpenStreamSync` and writes `ping`, like a real
   peer that starts its link handshake right away;
4. the test requires `listener.Accept()` to return within 5s, then checks the accepted
   connection reads `ping` and the peer reads back `pong`.

On the unpatched tree the test fails with:

```
--- FAIL: TestQUICListenerPeerWithoutStream (5.51s)
    link_quic_test.go:145: listener did not accept the second peer while the first peer had no stream
```

With the patch it passes in ~0.5s, including `-count=3 -race`.

## How it was verified

```
$ cd /tmp/work/ygg-quic                      # v0.5.14 tree + patch
$ GOFLAGS=-mod=mod GOPROXY=off go build ./...
# exit 0

$ GOFLAGS=-mod=mod GOPROXY=off go test ./src/core/ -run TestQUICListenerPeerWithoutStream -count=1 -v
--- PASS: TestQUICListenerPeerWithoutStream (0.51s)
ok  	github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/src/core	0.510s

$ GOFLAGS=-mod=mod GOPROXY=off go test ./src/core/ -count=1
ok  	github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/src/core	21.746s

$ GOFLAGS=-mod=mod GOPROXY=off go test ./src/core/ -run TestQUICListenerPeerWithoutStream -count=3 -race
ok  	github.com/yggdrasil-network/yggdrasil-go/src/core	2.570s

$ go vet ./src/core/     # clean
$ gofmt -l src/core/     # no output
```

The same test on the unpatched tree fails as quoted above (checked by reverting only
`link_quic.go` and re-running the test).

## Compatibility

- No wire-format change: `linkQUICStream`, the `ch` channel, the QUIC/TLS configura

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable error responses
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `errorResponse` object to the XHTTP inbound settings, replacing the bare status-only rejections with a service-consistent appearance.

Currently every rejected request is answered with a bare status code: no body, no `Content-Type` (Go's default "404 page not found" or nothing at all). From the terminating side (CDN, reverse proxy, monitoring) a server that answers *every* unknown path with a naked status code and no content type does not look like a normal service.

- `body` and `contentType` apply to every error response the hub writes (404 unknown path, 400/405/409/413/500 etc.), giving all rejections a uniform, service-consistent appearance.
- `statusCode` overrides the status for requests failing the padding validation — the effective authentication gate — allowing 403 semantics instead of the default 400.
- When `errorResponse` is unset, the behavior is unchanged.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "errorResponse": {
    "statusCode": 403,
    "body": "{\"error\":\"forbidden\"}",
    "contentType": "application/json"
  }
}
```

Resulting surface: unknown paths → `404 {"error":"forbidden"}`, the API gate without valid padding → `403` with the same body — a coherent API host instead of a bare 404/400 machine.

## Notes

- Server-side only. Round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 (matches all existing `.pb.go` headers; unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain).
- Proto field `errorResponse = 31` — merges cleanly alongside #7247 (`responseHeaders = 30`); both features are independent.

## Tests

- `Test_WriteErrorResponse`: bare default when unset, configured body + content type, padding-reject status default (400) and override (403).
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: DNS: honor nameserver timeouts for coalesced lookups
issues.body:
**Revised implementation:** [6ecd2853](https://github.com/eliotcougar/Xray-core/commit/6ecd2853f4af823312461b673ac733df21ad9754) · [complete focused diff against v26.10.21](https://github.com/eliotcougar/Xray-core/compare/1b1647cd9ddf0abc34b981d4611fc03bcac1ca74...6ecd2853f4af823312461b673ac733df21ad9754).

This PR was closed before the revised commits were pushed. Its Files changed view still shows the original head; the comparison above contains the implementation described here.

### Problem and practical effect

A foreground lookup can wait beyond its configured nameserver timeout when it joins an existing lookup for the same name and address family. In particular, an optimistic-cache refresh has an eight-second lifetime, while a foreground lookup may have a much shorter timeout. Blocking in `singleflight.Group.Do` delays returning to resolver selection and trying a healthy fallback.

The fix gives each waiter its own waiting lifetime and separates that from ownership of the shared operation. A short-lived waiter can leave promptly, while work needed by another waiter continues. It also prevents an earlier request's timeout from cancelling a shared query needed by a later request whose budget remains.

This is a nameserver-timeout correctness fix. The stable `LookupIP` interface remains context-free: closing an application connection does not automatically cancel its native DNS lookup. System-resolver cancellation is unchanged. No bulk-throughput or CPU improvement is claimed.

### Implementation

- Share queries per nameserver, domain and address family, with independent waiter contexts.
- Give the shared operation a bounded lifetime independent of the first waiter's deadline: eight seconds, extended for an explicitly longer nameserver timeout. Preserve routing context values.
- Cancel the operation when its last waiter leaves or DNS closes. A background refresh remains a waiter, retaining its existing eight-second policy.
- Handle A and AAAA independently, retaining a completed family when the other times out.
- Interrupt an owned TCP DNS connection on cancellation.
- Preserve single-family response TTLs and existing dual-stack TTL aggregation. Public interfaces and JSON configuration stay unchanged.

### Normal-configuration reproduction

Use an ordinary HTTP inbound and a freedom outbound with `streamSettings.sockopt.domainStrategy: "UseIPv4"`. The relevant DNS settings are:

```json
{
  "dns": {
    "queryStrategy": "UseIPv4",
    "enableParallelQuery": false,
    "servers": [
      {
        "address": "tcp+local://127.0.0.1:15353",
        "timeoutMs": 300,
        "serveStale": true,
        "serveExpiredTTL": 1
      },
      {
        "address": "tcp+local://127.0.0.1:15354",
        "timeoutMs": 300,
        "disableCache": true
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

Two controlled loopback DNS-over-TCP peers and a loopback HTTP origin make the sequence repeatable:

1. The primary returns the origin's IP with TTL 1, priming the cache.
2. After 1.15 seconds, an HTTP request receives the stale answer and starts a refresh. The primary delays this refresh by six seconds, then returns SERVFAIL; the fallback remains healthy.
3. After another 1.2 seconds, the stale answer is no longer eligible. A new request joins the refresh, despite having only a 300 ms nameserver budget.

Fresh Windows amd64 builds from the unmodified v26.10.21 base and the revised head produced these foreground completion times:

| Native configuration path | Unmodified | Revised |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Serial DNS, HTTP request | 4,804 ms | 328 ms |
| Parallel DNS, HTTP request | 4,813 ms | 326 ms |
| Serial DNS, UDP DNS outbound request | 4,805 ms | 304 ms |
| Parallel DNS, UDP DNS outbound request | 4,800 ms | 301 ms |

The parallel cases use distinct primary/fallback policy tags. All original refreshes completed; the primary received only priming plus refresh. These are controlled reproduction timings, not general network-performance estimates. No custom ca

issues.title: XHTTP: Add configurable response headers
issues.body:
## What

Adds an optional `responseHeaders` map (`map<string, string>`) to the XHTTP inbound settings, giving the server control over the headers it writes on responses.

Currently the hub hardcodes a set of response headers: the CORS block for the browser dialer (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`, `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`), `X-Accel-Buffering`, `Cache-Control` and the SSE `Content-Type`. With `responseHeaders` an operator can add, override, or remove any of them, as well as set arbitrary extra response headers.

## Semantics

- A key that doesn't collide with a default header is added to every response.
- A key that matches a hardcoded header overrides it.
- An empty value removes that header from the response entirely (including the hardcoded ones).
- When `responseHeaders` is unset, the behavior is byte-identical to before.

Example:

```json
"xhttpSettings": {
  "path": "/api/v2/stream",
  "responseHeaders": {
    "Server": "nginx",
    "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
    "Access-Control-Allow-Origin": "https://example.com",
    "X-Accel-Buffering": ""
  }
}
```

## Why

- The CORS headers only matter for the browser dialer; a plain server deployment currently emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` on every response, which is undesirable behind a specific origin and gets flagged by security reviews.
- Reverse-proxy and CDN setups sometimes require specific response headers (`Server`, `Via`, custom headers) or different cache semantics.
- Operators running behind intermediaries may want the response header set to stay consistent with the profile of the service they front, instead of carrying markers that no other service on that endpoint emits.

## Notes

- Server-side only; the client ignores it. It round-trips through `extra` like the other settings.
- `config.pb.go` regenerated with protoc v6.33.5 / protoc-gen-go v1.36.11 — the header matches all existing `.pb.go` files (`check-proto` passes; I verified the unmodified proto regenerates byte-identical with this toolchain first).

## Tests

- `Test_SetResponseHeader`: default / override / removal via empty value.
- `Test_WriteResponseHeader_ResponseHeaders`: CORS default, override, removal, custom header addition, origin echo.
- `go test ./...` passes locally across all packages, except the pre-existing network-dependent `TestQUICNameServer` in `app/dns`, which fails identically on pristine `main` in my environment (no QUIC egress).

issues.title: REALITY: authenticated handshake fails with `padding: -4` when the target sends an empty EncryptedExtensions (since v26.10.21)
issues.body:
### Integrity requirements

- [x] I have read all the comments in the issue template and ensured that this issue meet the requirements.
- [x] I confirm that I have read the documentation, understand the meaning of all the configuration items I wrote, and did not pile up seemingly useful options or default values.
- [x] I provided the complete config and logs, rather than just providing the truncated parts based on my own judgment.
- [x] I searched issues and did not find any similar issues.
- [x] The problem can be successfully reproduced in the latest Release

### Description

Since v26.10.21 (REALITY `83f621788ca8`), every authenticated REALITY connection fails when the target sends an **empty EncryptedExtensions** (no SNI ack, no ALPN, nothing else). With `"show": true` the server prints:

```
hs.handshake() err: payload[0]: 8, padding: -4
```

v26.9.9 (REALITY `8cdf7bf9c7f0`) works with the same target.

Cause:

- XTLS/REALITY `3c98159` ("Sync upstream Go 1.27+", #30) added to `handshake_server_tls13.go`:
  ```go
  if !hs.c.didResume && hs.clientHello.serverName != "" {
      encryptedExtensions.serverNameAck = true
  }
  ```
  An authenticated connection always carries SNI unless `serverNames` contains `""`, so REALITY's own EncryptedExtensions now always has the 4-byte empty `server_name` extension. Before this commit `encryptedExtensionsMsg` had no such field.
- `[REALITY] SECTION: mimic recorded handshakeLen` in `conn.go` pads each handshake record to the length recorded from the target and returns `payload[0]: %v, padding: %v` when its own record is longer (`payload[0]: 8` is EncryptedExtensions).
- REALITY's own EncryptedExtensions has no ALPN, so it is now 4 bytes longer than an empty one. A target whose EncryptedExtensions is empty gives a 28-byte record (including the 5-byte record header) against REALITY's 32, hence padding -4. Any extension on the target side (an SNI ack, ALPN, ...) is at least 4 bytes and absorbs it.

Not setting `serverNameAck` in the REALITY server (the pre-sync behaviour) looks sufficient, since padding then matches any target; I have not tested a patch.

This is easy to miss: the fallback path does not reach this code, so probing the node without the key looks fine, and without `show` the server logs only an Info line (`REALITY: processed invalid connection ...: handshake did not complete successfully`) while the client gets EOF. We hit it on a production node whose target neither acks SNI nor negotiates ALPN. To check a target, look for any extension besides `supported versions` and `key share`:

```
openssl s_client -connect <Domain>:443 -servername <Domain> -tls1_3 -alpn h2,http/1.1 -tlsextdebug </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep 'TLS server extension'
```

### Reproduction Method

All on loopback (Linux, OpenSSL 3.5.5). Three `openssl s_server` targets with the same self-signed certificate for `example.test`:

```
openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes -keyout k.pem -out c.pem -days 30 -subj /CN=example.test -addext subjectAltName=DNS:example.test
# A: empty EncryptedExtensions
openssl s_server -accept 127.0.0.1:20443 -cert c.pem -key k.pem -tls1_3 -www -quiet
# B: acks SNI (s_server acks only when -servername installs its callback and the name matches)
openssl s_server -accept 127.0.0.1:20444 -cert c.pem -key k.pem -tls1_3 -www -quiet -servername example.test -cert2 c.pem -key2 k.pem
# C: no SNI ack, but negotiates ALPN
openssl s_server -accept 127.0.0.1:20445 -cert c.pem -key k.pem -tls1_3 -www -quiet -alpn h2,http/1.1
# something to fetch through the proxy
python3 -m http.server 18080 --bind 127.0.0.1
```

Start the server (config below, `target` pointing at A, B or C) and the client (always v26.10.21), then `curl -x socks5h://127.0.0.1:11080 http://127.0.0.1:18080/`:

| server | target | target EE record | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| v26.10.21 | A | 28 | curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer; `padding: -4` |
| v26.10.21 | B | 32 | 200 |

Direct/Freedom outbound: Close blocked connections after `blockDelay` (VLESS, Hysteria, etc.)
issues.body:
Regression from #6060 (958eb9e). `blackhole` waits for `buf.Copy(input, buf.Discard)` and relies on the `blockDelay` timer calling `common.Interrupt(input)` to end it. That only works for a pipe: VLESS, Hysteria and other inbounds that use `DispatchLink` pass a reader on the client connection, and `Interrupt` does nothing to it. So a blocked connection stays open until the client closes it, whatever `blockDelay` is. In our tests it was still open after 330 s, longer than `connIdle`.

Drain the input in a goroutine and return once the delay has passed or the input has ended. The inbound then closes the connection, as it does after the blackhole outbound.

`TestVlessBlockDelay` covers `blockDelay` 0 and 1 through a VLESS inbound. Both cases fail on main.

issues.title: Windows: core fails to start with 'The system cannot find the path specified' when the working directory contains a directory junction (regression in v26.10.21)
issues.body:
### Describe the bug

On Windows, Xray fails to start when the **current working directory** contains a directory junction:

```
Failed to start: main: failed to load config files: [config.json] > infra/conf/serial: failed to read config: &{Name:config.json Format:json} > The system cannot find the path specified.
```

The config file itself exists and is readable — the failure happens while Xray resolves the path of an already opened file.

### Versions

- Xray core **v26.10.21** (go1.27.3 windows/amd64) — broken
- Xray core **v26.9.30** — works (the code path described below does not exist there)

### Steps to reproduce

```bat
mkdir C:\test\target
echo {}> C:\test\target\config.json
mklink /J C:\test\link C:\test\target

cd /d C:\test\link
xray run -c config.json
```

Result:

```
Xray 26.10.21 (Xray, Penetrates Everything.) 1b1647c (go1.27.3 windows/amd64)
[Info] infra/conf/serial: Reading config: &{Name:config.json Format:json}
Failed to start: main: failed to load config files: [config.json] > infra/conf/serial: failed to read config: &{Name:config.json Format:json} > The system cannot find the path specified.
```

With the **physical** path it works:

```bat
cd /d C:\test\target
xray run -c config.json
[Info] infra/conf/serial: Reading config: &{Name:config.json Format:json}
[Warning] core: Xray 26.10.21 started
```

### Root cause

`main/confloader/external/external.go`, function `readConfigFile()` (introduced in v26.10.21):

```go
path, err := filepath.Abs(file.Name())
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
path, err = filepath.EvalSymlinks(path)
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
switch strings.ToLower(filepath.Ext(path)) {
case ".jsonc", ".json", ".yml", ".yaml", ".toml", ".pb", ".protobuf":
default:
    return nil, errors.New("unsupported config file extension: ", path)
}
```

`filepath.EvalSymlinks` fails on Windows with `ERROR_PATH_NOT_FOUND` ("The system cannot find the path specified") as soon as one component of the path is a **directory junction** (this is a Go standard library behavior, see the related golang/go report).

Notes:
- the file has already been opened successfully at this point (`os.Open(arg)` succeeded);
- the resolved path is only used for an **extension whitelist** check, so the resolution itself is not required;
- the failure is fatal and prevents the core from starting at all.

### Impact

Every user whose Xray is launched with a working directory located under a junction / symlinked directory is affected, e.g.:

- Scoop: `C:\Users\<user>\scoop\apps\<app>\current` is a junction to the versioned folder;
- Chocolatey / WinGet shim directories;
- any manually created `mklink /J` layout.

This is not only a CLI issue: for example **v2rayN** (which starts the core with `run -c config.json` and `WorkingDirectory = <install dir>\binConfigs`) becomes completely unusable after updating the bundled core to v26.10.21 — the client shows `Failed to start: main: failed to load config files: [config.json] ... The system cannot find the path specified.` and no proxy is available.

### Suggested fix

Do not let the symlink resolution failure be fatal — fall back to the unresolved path and check the extension with `filepath.Ext`:

```go
path, err := filepath.Abs(file.Name())
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
if resolved, err := filepath.EvalSymlinks(path); err == nil {
    path = resolved
}
switch strings.ToLower(filepath.Ext(path)) {
case ".jsonc", ".json", ".yml", ".yaml", ".toml", ".pb", ".protobuf":
default:
    return nil, errors.New("unsupported config file extension: ", path)
}
```

### Minimal Go reproducer for the underlying behavior

```go
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
)

func main() {
	p, err := filepath.Abs(os.Args[1])
	fmt.Println("Abs:         ", p, err)
	r, err := filepath.EvalSymlinks(p)
	fmt.Println("EvalSymlinks:", r, err)
}
```

Run it with the CWD set to a junction directory and pass a file name inside it:

```bat
cd /d C:\test\link
go run main.go config.json
`

issues.title: WebSocket: Treat normal close frames as io.EOF
issues.body:
## What this fixes

A WebSocket close frame with a normal status (1000) or no status (1005) ends the byte stream the same way a FIN does, but `connection.Read` surfaced gorilla's `*websocket.CloseError` to its callers.

VLESS and Trojan carry payload without framing, so a response copy ended with that error. `app/proxyman/outbound.Handler.Dispatch` treats every error other than `io.EOF` as a failure and calls `common.Interrupt`, which releases the data still buffered in the pipe before the inbound has read it. The client gets a short response that ends with a normal FIN - silent truncation for HTTP/1.0 responses without Content-Length, and a `websocket: close 1000 (normal)` line for every such connection.

Fix: map `websocket.IsCloseError(err, CloseNormalClosure, CloseNoStatusReceived)` to `io.EOF` in `connection.Read`. Other close codes keep their error semantics. The same wrapper is used by the XHTTP browser dialer client (`transport/internet/splithttp/browser_client.go`), so that path inherits the fix.

Fixes #7235.

## Test record

Environment: `1b1647cd` (v26.10.21), linux/amd64. The configs and scripts from the report used verbatim: target answers `HTTP/1.0 200 OK` + 65536 body bytes without Content-Length, then closes; the client fetches through an `http` inbound -> VLESS/ws outbound.

| scenario | base `1b1647cd` | with fix `bba46a28` |
|---|---|---|
| 20 sequential fetches, `GOMAXPROCS=1` | 19/20 short (15 x 0 B, 2 x 32749 B, 1 x 8171 B, 1 x 8173 B); 20 `close 1000` log lines | 20/20 complete 65536 B; 0 close lines |
| 10 rounds x 20 concurrent fetches | ~172/200 short; 200 `close 1000` log lines | 200/200 complete; 0 close lines |
| raw TCP control (same scripts) | 20/20 complete; 0 close lines | 20/20 complete |

The byte counts above are from the runs saved for this report; a second base run produced the same shape (18/20 short) with a different byte split.

Unit tests (new `connection_test.go`, real WebSocket server + the production wrapper): RED on base - close 1000 and 1005 come back as `websocket: close 1000 (normal)` / `close 1005 (no status)` instead of `io.EOF`; GREEN with the fix. A 1001 (`going away`) control asserts that other close codes stay errors, before and after.

`go test ./transport/internet/...` - 25 packages pass. `go build ./...`, `gofmt`, `go vet` clean.

Known boundary: a close frame arriving in the middle of a fragmented message still surfaces as a close error, because that payload is genuinely incomplete; only a close after a complete message is remapped, which is the reported mechanism.

issues.title: Sniffer: Don't count reads without new data as attempts
issues.body:
## Problem

TLS sniffing on a VLESS + Vision server almost always fails when the traffic comes through another Xray server with VLESS + Vision (a proxy chain). `routeOnly` gets no domain, and the connection is routed by IP only.

```
client → server 1 → server 2 → internet
```

All hops use VLESS + REALITY + `xtls-rprx-vision`. Server 2 has sniffing on the inbound and domain rules above an IP rule:

```json
"sniffing": { "enabled": true, "destOverride": ["http", "tls", "quic"], "routeOnly": true }
```
```json
{ "domain": ["geosite:habr"], "outboundTag": "direct-out" },
{ "ip": ["geoip:ru"], "outboundTag": "block-out" }
```

Opening https://habr.com in Chrome is blocked by the `geoip:ru` rule. The server 2 log has no `sniffed domain:` line for any `:443` connection, and the routing decision is made in under a millisecond, without waiting for the 200 ms sniffing deadline:

```
proxy/vless/inbound: firstLen = 1186
proxy/vless/inbound: received request for tcp:178.248.237.68:443
from 0.0.0.0:0 accepted tcp:178.248.237.68:443 [vless-tcp-reality-os-in -> block-out]
app/dispatcher: taking detour [block-out] for [tcp:178.248.237.68:443]
```

When the client connects to server 2 directly, the domain is sniffed.

## Root cause

1. **TLS record size.** `crypto/tls`, uTLS and REALITY use dynamic record sizing: for the first 128 KB of a connection a record is limited to `tcpMSSEstimate = 1208` bytes. In TLS 1.3 that leaves 1208 − 5 (record header) − 16 (AEAD tag) − 1 (inner content type) = **1186 bytes** of plaintext per record, which is the `firstLen = 1186` above.
2. **Client → server 1.** The client sends the whole ClientHello (~1.7–2 KB with `X25519MLKEM768`) as one Vision frame. The first record carries 44 bytes of VLESS request header, 21 bytes of Vision frame header and the first 1121 bytes of the ClientHello; the second record carries the rest of it plus padding. Server 1 reads the ClientHello as two chunks: 1121 bytes and the remainder.
3. **Server 1 → server 2.** The VLESS outbound on server 1 writes each chunk as a separate Vision frame with its own padding. For the first frame, 44 + 21 + 1121 = 1186 bytes fill the first record exactly, so the frame's padding goes into a record of its own. With the default testseed `{900, 500, 900, 256}`, content of 900 bytes or more gets 0–255 bytes of padding, so this happens unless the padding is 0, i.e. in about 255 of 256 connections.
4. **VisionReader on server 2.** For the padding-only record, [`VisionReader.ReadMultiBuffer`](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/1b1647cd9ddf0abc34b981d4611fc03bcac1ca74/proxy/proxy.go#L235-L243) strips the padding and returns an empty `MultiBuffer` with a nil error.
5. **Sniffer.** `cachedReader.Cache` gets no new data, but the [sniffing loop](https://github.com/XTLS/Xray-core/blob/1b1647cd9ddf0abc34b981d4611fc03bcac1ca74/app/dispatcher/default.go#L392-L421) runs the sniffers again on the same 1121 bytes. `SniffTLS` returns `ErrNoClue` again, because the TLS record is still incomplete, and the second `ErrNoClue` ends sniffing with `errSniffingTimeout`. The rest of the ClientHello arrives with the next read, too late.

Without server 1 there is no padding-only record between the two parts of the ClientHello, so two reads are enough.

## Reproduction

The chain was reproduced on one machine:

- Everything runs in an unprivileged network namespace (`unshare -rn`) with loopback MTU 1500.
- A local HTTPS server plays both `habr.com` and the REALITY target.
- **Client:** SOCKS inbound with sniffing and `routeOnly`, VLESS + REALITY + Vision outbound to server 1, or directly to server 2.
- **Server 1:** VLESS + REALITY + Vision inbound without sniffing, VLESS + REALITY + Vision outbound to server 2.
- **Server 2:** VLESS + REALITY + Vision inbound with sniffing and `routeOnly`. `domain:habr.com` goes to `freedom`, redirected to the local server; `0.0.0.0/0` and `::/0` go to `blackhole`.

comments.issue_title: DNS: honor nameserver timeouts for coalesced lookups
comments.body:
Hi @Meo597, I’m Codex, the AI coding agent working with Eliot. Thank you for raising the context-ownership and native DNS-path concerns.

Rechecking the original approach exposed a real ownership problem: releasing an individual waiter was insufficient while the first caller still owned the shared upstream request. The revised implementation now gives the shared operation an independent, bounded lifetime, keeps each waiter's deadline separate, and cancels shared work when its last waiter leaves or DNS closes. A/AAAA work is shared separately, and the stale-refresh, parallel-query and DNS-outbound paths were checked independently of adjacent application changes. A single-family TTL regression found during that review has also been fixed.

Your point about `LookupIP` lacking caller context remains valid. The revised description now limits the claim to respecting internal nameserver timeouts and preserving other waiters. In a normal JSON-configured stale-refresh reproduction, HTTP and UDP DNS-outbound requests completed in approximately 301–328 ms with a 300 ms timeout, versus about 4.8 seconds on the unmodified base. The HTTP/2 checks reused one connection; this is a waiting-lifetime issue rather than a connection-pooling performance claim.

Would you be willing to review the [revised focused diff](https://github.com/eliotcougar/Xray-core/compare/1b1647cd9ddf0abc34b981d4611fc03bcac1ca74...6ecd2853f4af823312461b673ac733df21ad9754), particularly the lifetime policy and its interaction with those native DNS paths?

I’ve updated the title and description and left the PR closed following your decision. GitHub’s closed-PR diff still shows the earlier head, so the link above points directly to the tested revision, `6ecd2853`. If the revised approach is worth pursuing, please let us know whether you would prefer this PR reopened for review.

comments.issue_title: REALITY: authenticated handshake fails with `padding: -4` when the target sends an empty EncryptedExtensions (since v26.10.21)
comments.body:
Reproduced this at `1b1647cd` and tested the patch the report says was not tried yet (dropping the ack in REALITY's server). It clears the failure, and the two targets that work today keep working.

Rig is the report's, on loopback with OpenSSL 3.5.5: xray client -> vless + `xtls-rprx-vision` + reality -> v26.10.21 server with `"show": true`; targets A (empty EncryptedExtensions), B (`-servername example.test -cert2 ...`, acks SNI), C (`-alpn h2,http/1.1`); `curl -x socks5h://...` to a local `http.server` through the `finalRules` allow rule.

| build | target A | target B | target C |
|---|---|---|---|
| v26.10.21, untouched reality pin | 0/2, `padding: -4` x10 | 2/2 | 2/2 |
| v26.10.21 + the hunk below | 2/2, no padding line | 2/2 | 2/2 |

The entire change, in XTLS/REALITY `handshake_server_tls13.go` (the block `3c98159` added):

```diff
-	if !hs.c.didResume && hs.clientHello.serverName != "" {
-		encryptedExtensions.serverNameAck = true
-	}
```

With it REALITY's own EncryptedExtensions is 28 bytes and matches an empty target EE; on target B the same record is 4 bytes shorter than the target's, and the mimic pads positively as it always did. Nothing else in the server path reads that field.

Client side is safe for the same reason the reporter gives: `handshake_client_tls13.go` only rejects an ack the client did not ask for (`hs.hello.serverName == ""`), an xray REALITY client always sends SNI, and both B and C still complete against the patched server.

I did not touch XTLS/REALITY and have not proposed a parallel fix anywhere: the module pin is `83f621788ca8` and my build used a local `replace`. So landing it means a REALITY commit plus a `go.mod` bump here; the matrix above is what that bump would be validated against.

comments.issue_title: REALITY: authenticated handshake fails with `padding: -4` when the target sends an empty EncryptedExtensions (since v26.10.21)
comments.body:
The tempting fix in the mimic layer is the wrong layer. Clamping a negative padding to zero lets a 32 byte EncryptedExtensions go out against a 28 byte recorded one, and the rest of the flight is sliced off the recorded stream in order, so Certificate and everything after it shifts by the same 4 bytes. Dropping serverNameAck on the REALITY side, as you suggest, keeps every later message on its recorded offset, not just this one. It is also safe on the client side: the server_name acknowledgment in EncryptedExtensions is empty and optional, and nothing in the client handshake depends on receiving it.

Is this regression being taken internally, or are you open to someone outside picking it up?

comments.body:
Reproduced on current main (`1b1647c`, linux/amd64; the configs and scripts from the report used verbatim).

**Repro, base build, 20 sequential fetches with `GOMAXPROCS=1`:**
- VLESS over ws: 19 of 20 short (run 1: 14 x 0 bytes, 3 x 8171, 2 x 32749, 1 complete; run 2: 11 x 0, 3 x 8171, 1 x 32749, 1 x 49133, 1 x 57325, 1 x 8173, 2 complete), and all 20 connections log `websocket: close 1000 (normal)`.
- Control raw TCP, same build and scripts: 20/20 complete at 65536 bytes, zero close-error lines.

**Trace agrees with the report:** in `transport/internet/websocket/connection.go`, `Read` -> `getReader` -> `c.conn.NextReader()` returns gorilla's `*websocket.CloseError` for close frames 1000/1005, while a byte-stream reader expects `io.EOF` there. `app/proxyman/outbound.Handler.Dispatch` then treats it as a failure and calls `common.Interrupt`, which releases the data still buffered in the pipe before the inbound has taken it - the truncated tail.

**Plan:** map `websocket.IsCloseError(err, websocket.CloseNormalClosure, websocket.CloseNoStatusReceived)` to `io.EOF` in `connection.Read`; other close codes (1001, 1006, ...) stay errors. Regression test at the connection level (close 1000 and 1005 -> `io.EOF`; 1001/1006 still errors) plus the end-to-end repro above and the raw/VMess controls. Happy to go a different way if you would rather handle this in the Dispatch/pipe layer instead.

## Update: root trigger identified and workaround confirmed

**Confirmed workaround:** changing the XRay Reality fingerprint from `chrome` to `firefox` immediately restores traffic.

Broken configuration:

```json
"realitySettings": {
  "fingerprint": "chrome"
}
```

Working configuration:

```json
"realitySettings": {
  "fingerprint": "firefox"
}
```

No server-side changes were required.

This workaround has now been confirmed on my OPPO CPH2701 as well. Other users in this issue have reported the same general failure on Samsung, Redmi, and Infinix devices.

Important control result:

* The original configuration with `fingerprint: chrome` still works correctly using standalone Xray-core 26.3.27 in Termux on the same phone.
* The same configuration does not pass traffic through AmneziaVPN.
* Changing only the fingerprint to `firefox` makes AmneziaVPN work immediately.

Therefore, the issue appears to be related specifically to the handling or implementation of the `chrome` Reality/uTLS fingerprint in the XRay version bundled with AmneziaVPN, rather than to the server, routing, DNS, or Android VPNService in general.

This is a workaround, not a complete fix: existing profiles using `fingerprint: chrome` can still silently fail while AmneziaVPN reports `Connected`.



**Describe the bug**

AmneziaVPN on Android shows `Connected` for a self-hosted XRay/VLESS/Reality profile, but the VPN tunnel is not actually usable.

The Android VPN interface is created, routes are installed, and Amnezia starts `tun2Socks` and `XRay`. However, real application traffic is blackholed: TCP connect succeeds, but HTTP/TLS payload does not receive any response.

The same XRay/VLESS/Reality configuration works correctly when launched manually with standalone `xray-core` inside Termux on the same phone. A different commercial VPN application also works correctly as a full-system VPN on the same device.

So this does not look like a server/config/network problem. It looks like an issue in AmneziaVPN Android's XRay/tun2socks/VPNService data-plane on this OPPO / Android 16 device.

The issue started suddenly on two identical OPPO phones on the same day.

---

**To Reproduce**

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Install AmneziaVPN on OPPO CPH2701 / Android 16.
2. Add a self-hosted XRay / VLESS / Reality profile.
3. Disable app split tunneling.
4. Disable site/IP split tunneling.
5. Disable Android Private DNS.
6. Make sure Always-on VPN / kill switch is disabled.
7. Connect to the XRay server.
8. AmneziaVPN UI shows `Connected`.
9. Run diagnostics from Termux.

TCP connect succeeds:

```bash
nc -vz -w5 1.1.1.1 80
nc -vz -w5 1.1.1.1 443

Connection to 1.1.1.1 80 port [tcp/http] succeeded!
Connection to 1.1.1.1 443 port [tcp/https] succeeded!
Connection to 8.8.8.8 443 port [tcp/https] succeeded!
```

But HTTP/TLS payload does not work:

```bash

```

Result:

```text

* Established connection to 1.1.1.1 from 10.0.42.2
> GET / HTTP/1.1
> Host: 1.1.1.1
> User-Agent: curl/...

* Operation timed out after 15003 milliseconds with 0 bytes received

issues.body:
Fixes #2248.

Currently, when connecting to a WireGuard server on Windows with a large split-tunnel list (e.g. the 11k-CIDR RU list from #2248), the client spends 5–20 minutes on "Connecting" before it finally reports "Connected". The same profile connects in 1–3 seconds on macOS, Android and iOS. Even after the first connect succeeds, reconnecting in the same session hangs on "Connecting" indefinitely.

This happens because `Daemon::activate` installs exclusion routes one at a time: every `CreateIpForwardEntry2` call wakes `wcmSvc` (which `router_win.cpp` already works around for OpenVPN/Shadowsocks but not for WireGuard), and `WindowsRouteMonitor::addExclusionRoute` re-fetches the full routing table and re-runs `updateCapturedRoutes` for every prefix. On top of that, `NotifyRouteChange2` fires a callback per row during interface bring-up; each callback queues a `routeChanged` slot that rescans everything, and Wintun's subnet-broadcast `/32` entries (which `QHostAddress::isBroadcast()` does not recognize) keep failing with `ERROR_OBJECT_ALREADY_EXISTS` and get retried on every rescan - the daemon event loop fills up and `Daemon::checkHandshake()` never gets a slot, so the `connected` signal never reaches the GUI.

This PR adds batch entry points to `WireguardUtils` so `WindowsRouteMonitor` can install all exclusion prefixes against one routing-table snapshot per address family and suspend `wcmSvc` for the whole batch (matching `router_win.cpp`), debounces `NotifyRouteChange2` callbacks through a 50 ms single-shot timer so bursts collapse into one rescan, and pins prefixes that return `ERROR_OBJECT_ALREADY_EXISTS` so they stop being retried. Other platforms fall back to the existing per-prefix path and are untouched.

Update: disconnect/reconnect and server switch now also remove routes in one batch with wcmSvc suspended, and a gateway change no longer rewrites all exclusion routes with wcmSvc running. Also fixes: routes covered by a removed exclusion were not re-captured (inverted check in updateCapturedRoutes), a colliding prefix stayed outside the tunnel permanently, and switchServer did not remove CIDR exclusions of the previous server.

issues.title: macOS: site-based split tunneling is not applied for AWG/WireGuard — always full tunnel
issues.body:
# macOS: Site-based split tunneling is not applied for AWG/WireGuard — always full tunnel

## Environment

- AmneziaVPN client: **5.0.3.0** (macOS pkg, universal)
- OS: **macOS 27.0.1** (Apple Silicon, arm64)
- Protocol: **AWG** (self-hosted server, amneziawg-tools v3.1.20260812)
- GUI state: Settings → Split tunneling → Sites → **"Only for selected sites"** (`Conf.routeMode = 1`, `Conf.ForwardSites` populated with 36 domains), VPN reconnected after the change

## Summary

On macOS, for AWG (and WireGuard) connections, the site-based split tunneling settings are **silently ignored** — the connection is always full tunnel. Two independent code paths cause this:

### 1. Route-split logic is skipped for AWG/WG containers

`client/vpnConnection.cpp` (`VpnConnection::onConnectionStateChanged`, Connected branch) wraps the **entire** split-tunneling route logic in:

```cpp
// line 135
if (!ContainerUtils::isAwgContainer(container) && container != DockerContainer::WireGuard) {
    ...
    if (m_appSettingsRepository->isSitesSplitTunnelingEnabled()) {
        // routeDeleteList("0.0.0.0"), VpnOnlyForwardSites -> addSitesRoutes(),
        // VpnAllExceptSites -> 0.0.0.0/1 + 128.0.0.0/1 ...
    }
}
```

For AWG and WireGuard containers none of this ever runs: neither forward-site routes (include mode) nor exception routes (exclude mode) are added, and the DNS servers are not excluded from the tunnel on macOS.

### 2. Client config is hardcoded to full tunnel

`client/core/configurators/wireguardConfigurator.cpp` (line 275):

```cpp
clientConfig.allowedIps = QStringList { "0.0.0.0/0", "::/0" };
```

This is unconditional — the configured split-tunneling mode is not reflected in `AllowedIPs`. The macOS daemon then expands the default route into two halves (`client/platforms/macos/daemon/wireguardutilsmacos.cpp`, `updateRoutePrefix`, line 357):

```cpp
return m_rtmonitor->insertRoute(IPAddress("0.0.0.0/1")) &&
       m_rtmonitor->insertRoute(IPAddress("128.0.0.0/1"));
```

So every AWG connection gets `0/1` + `128.0/1` → tunnel, i.e. full tunnel, regardless of GUI state.

### 3. Related: `routeGateway()` is never set for WG/AWG

`VpnProtocol::routeGateway()` is only populated by the OpenVPN (`openVpnProtocol.cpp:172,178`) and Xray (`xrayProtocol.cpp:33`) protocols. For WireGuard/AWG it stays empty. The macOS-only branch in the `VpnAllExceptSites` path relies on it:

```cpp
#ifdef Q_OS_MACOS
    iface->routeAddList(m_vpnProtocol->routeGateway(), QStringList() << dns1 << dns2);
#endif
    addSitesRoutes(m_vpnProtocol->routeGateway(), routeMode);
```

— so even for protocols where the split logic runs, on macOS the DNS exclusion routes and site routes are added via an **empty gateway** whenever the protocol is WG/AWG (`routeAddList("", ip)` silently fails).

## Steps to reproduce

1. macOS 27.0.1 (arm64), AmneziaVPN 5.0.3.0, self-hosted AWG server
2. Settings → Split tunneling → Sites → mode "Only for selected sites", add e.g. `youtube.com`
3. Connect via AWG
4. `route -n get alfabank.ru` (not in the list) → `interface: utunX` (tunnel) — expected `en0`
5. `route -n get youtube.com` → `interface: utunX` — this one is correct, but only because everything is routed into the tunnel

## Actual result

- `route -n get default` → en0, but `0/1` + `128.0/1` → utun (full tunnel in practice)
- Sites **not** in the forward list (including the configured DNS servers, e.g. 1.1.1.1) are routed through the tunnel
- GUI split-tunneling settings have **no effect** on AWG connections
